<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Consumer loans may entail greater credit risk than residential mortgage loans, particularly in the case of consumer loans which are unsecured or are secured by rapidly depreciable assets, such as automobiles. In addition, consumer loan collections are dependent on the borrower&#8217;s continuing financial stability, and thus are more likely to be affected by adverse personal circumstances as well as the current slowing economy. Furthermore, the application of various federal and state laws, including bankruptcy and insolvency laws, may limit the amount which can be recovered on such loans. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we had no repossessed automobiles. There</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">were no non-performing consumer loans at December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>. While the current amount of our repossessed assets and non-performing consumer loans is low, there can be no assurance that delinquencies in our consumer loan portfolio will not increase in the future. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Originations, Sales and Purchases of Loans </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We originate real estate and other loans through our loan officers, marketing efforts, our customer base, walk-in customers and referrals from real estate brokers, builders, attorneys and others in the community. We occasionally offer incentives to employees for these loan referrals. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">From time to time we sell loans based on asset/liability, risk-sharing and regulatory considerations. For instance, we may sell</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">participation interests in our large multi-family, commercial real estate and commercial loans in order to diversify our risk or</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">accommodate a borrower with a need in excess of our legal lending limit. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we do not service any&nbsp;<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family loans for others. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We have purchased, and may purchase in the future, loans from third parties to supplement loan production. In particular, we may purchase loans of a type which are not available to us with favorable terms in our own market area. &nbsp;In <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we purchased $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">5.5</font> million in participations with other institutions. We generally use the same underwriting and approval standards in evaluating loan purchases as we do in originating loans. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, approximately $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">11.2</font> million of our loan portfolio was serviced by others. While we intend to focus on internally generated originations, we may from time to time purchase participations in multi-family, commercial real estate and commercial loans with other financial institutions. The following table shows our loan origination, purchase and principal repayment activity during the periods indicated. Loans are presented net of loans in process and the allowance for loan losses. We did not sell any loans during the periods covered by the table. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Asset Quality </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Delinquency Procedures</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> When a borrower fails to make a required payment on a loan, we attempt to cause the delinquency to be cured by contacting the borrower. A late notice is generated and is sent to all mortgage loans <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">15</font> days delinquent and to all consumer loans <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font> days delinquent. The borrower is contacted within at least <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font> days after the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> date of all loans. Another late notice along with any required demand letters as set forth in the loan contract are sent <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">30</font> days after the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> date. Additional written and verbal contacts may be made with the borrower between <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">30</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">60</font> days after the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> date. If the delinquency is not cured by the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">60</font>th day, the customer is normally provided <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">30</font> days written notice that the account will be referred to counsel for collection and foreclosure, if necessary. If it becomes necessary to foreclose, the property is sold at public sale and we may bid on the property to protect our interest. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">All loan charge-offs are recommended and approved by the Bank&#8217;s Loan Monitoring Committee or its Risk Rating sub-committee and ratified by our President or the Chief Executive Officer. Our procedures for repossession and sale of collateral are subject to various requirements under Illinois state consumer protection laws. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">When we acquire real estate as a result of foreclosure or by deed in lieu of foreclosure it is classified as a repossessed asset until it is sold. The real estate is recorded at estimated fair value, less estimated cost to sell, at the date of acquisition, and any write-down resulting from the acquisition is charged to the allowance for loan losses. Subsequent decreases in the value of the property are recorded through expense. After acquisition, all rental income is recognized through increases in non-interest income, while costs incurred in maintaining the property are recorded through expense. Costs relating to the development and improvement of the property, however, are capitalized to the extent of estimated fair value less estimated costs to sell. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Classified Assets</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">. Federal regulations provide for the classification of loans and other assets, such as debt and equity securities, considered to be of lesser quality as &#8220;substandard,&#8221; &#8220;doubtful&#8221; or &#8220;loss.&#8221; An asset is considered &#8220;substandard&#8221; if it is inadequately protected by the current net worth and paying capacity of the obligor or of the collateral pledged, if any. &#8220;Substandard&#8221; assets include those characterized by the &#8220;distinct possibility&#8221; that the insured institution will sustain &#8220;some loss&#8221; if the deficiencies are not corrected. Assets classified as &#8220;doubtful&#8221; have all of the weaknesses inherent in those classified &#8220;substandard,&#8221; with the added characteristic that the weaknesses present make &#8220;collection or liquidation in full,&#8221; on the basis of currently existing facts, conditions, and values, &#8220;highly questionable and improbable.&#8221; Assets classified as &#8220;loss&#8221; are those considered &#8220;uncollectible&#8221; and of such little value that their continuance as assets without the establishment of a specific loss allowance is not warranted. Assets which do not currently expose the insured institution to sufficient risk to warrant classification in <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> of the aforementioned categories but possess weaknesses are designated as &#8220;special mention&#8221; by our management. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">When an insured institution classifies problem assets as either substandard or doubtful, it performs an impairment analysis and charges off the impaired portion of the loan through the allowance for loan and lease losses. Under certain instances, the bank may establish specific loss allowances in an amount deemed prudent by management to cover probable incurred losses. General allowances represent loss allowances which have been established to cover probable incurred losses associated with lending activities, but which, unlike specific allowances, have not been allocated to particular problem assets. When an insured institution classifies problem assets or portions of assets as &#8220;loss,&#8221; it is required to charge-off the impaired amount. An institution&#8217;s determination as to the classification of its assets and the amount of its valuation allowances is subject to review by the regulatory authorities, who may order the establishment of additional general or specific loss allowances. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In accordance with our classification of assets policy, we regularly review the problem loans in our portfolio to determine whether any loans require classification in accordance with applicable regulations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Non-Performing Assets. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We cease accruing interest on our loans when contractual payments of principal or interest have become <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">90</font> days past <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> on non-consumer secured loans, and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">120</font> days past <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> on consumer loans as per Interagency Guidance on Uniform Retail Credit Classification and Account Management Policy, or if management has serious doubts about further collectability of principal or interest, even though the loan is currently performing. A loan may remain on accrual status if it is in the process of collection and is either guaranteed or well secured. When a loan is placed on nonaccrual status, unpaid interest credited to income is reversed. Generally, loans are restored to accrual status when the obligation is brought current, has performed in accordance with the contractual terms for a reasonable period of time and the ultimate collectability of the total contractual principal and interest is no longer in doubt. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Non-performing Loans.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, our non-performing loans, other than non-accruing troubled debt restructurings described below, totaling $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">1.5</font> million, includes a&nbsp;<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family loan, one multi-family loan, and one commercial real estate loan.&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">For the years ended December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>, interest income that would have been recorded had our non-accruing loans been current in accordance with their original terms was immaterial. No interest income was recognized on such loans for the years ended December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Troubled Debt Restructurings.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Troubled debt restructurings are loan restructurings in which we, for economic or legal reasons related to an existing borrower&#8217;s financial difficulties, grant a concession to the debtor that we would not otherwise consider. Typically, a troubled debt restructuring involves a modification of terms of a debt, such as reduction of the stated interest rate for the remaining original life of the debt, extension of the maturity date at a stated interest rate lower than the current market rate for new debt with similar risk, reduction of the face amount of the debt, or reduction of accrued interest. We consider modifications only after analyzing the borrower&#8217;s current repayment capacity, evaluating the strength of any guarantors based on documented current financial information, and assessing the current value of any collateral pledged. These modifications are made only when there is a reasonable and attainable workout plan that has been agreed to by the borrower and that is in our best interests. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Loans on non-accrual status at the date of modification are initially classified as non-accrual troubled debt restructurings. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>, we had $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">345,000</font> and $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">415,000</font> in non-accruing troubled debt restructurings, respectively. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, non-accrual troubled debt restructurings included a single <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family residential loan for $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">61,000</font> and one multi-family loan for $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">284,000</font>.</font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Our policy provides that troubled debt restructured loans are returned to accrual status after a period of satisfactory and reasonable future payment performance under the terms of the restructuring. Satisfactory payment performance is generally no less than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">six</font> consecutive months of timely payments and demonstrated ability to continue to repay. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>, we</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">had $1.2 million and $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.5</font> million in accruing troubled debt restructurings, respectively. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, accruing troubled debt restructurings included <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family residential loans totaling $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">526,000</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> multi-family loan totaling $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">705,000</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">million</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">collateralized by a&nbsp;<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font> unit apartment building. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">For the years ended December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>, interest income that would have been recorded had our troubled debt restructurings been current in accordance with their original terms was $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">93,000</font>&nbsp;and $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">131,000</font>, respectively. Interest income recognized on such loans for the years ended December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font> was $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">68,000</font> and $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">98,000</font>, respectively. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Other Loans of Concern. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, there were no other loans or other assets that are not disclosed above, including criticized and non-performing assets, where known information about the possible credit problems of borrowers caused us to have serious doubts as to the ability of the borrowers to comply with present loan repayment terms and which may result in disclosure of such loans in the future. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Allowance for Loan Losses </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Analysis and Determination of the Allowance for Loan Losses</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">. Our allowance for loan losses is the amount considered necessary to absorb probable incurred losses in our loan portfolio at the balance sheet date. We evaluate the need to establish loss allowances against losses on loans on a quarterly basis. When additional allowances are necessary, a provision for loan losses is charged to earnings. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Our methodology for assessing the appropriateness of the allowance for loan losses consists of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> key elements: (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">specific valuation allowances for individually impaired loans and (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">a general valuation allowance on the remainder of the loan portfolio. Although we determine the amount of each element of the allowance separately, the entire allowance for loan losses is available for the entire portfolio. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Specific Allowances for Impaired Loans</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">. We establish a specific allowance when loans are determined to be impaired. Loss is measured by determining the present value of expected future cash flows or, for collateral-dependent loans, the fair value of the collateral less selling cost. Factors in identifying a specific problem loan include: (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the strength of the customer&#8217;s personal or business cash flows; (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the availability of other sources of repayment; (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">3</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the amount <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> or past <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font>; (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">4</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the type and value of collateral; (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">5</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the strength of our collateral position; (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">6</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the estimated cost to sell the collateral; and (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">7</font>)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the borrower&#8217;s effort to cure the delinquency. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">General Valuation Allowance on the Remainder of the Loan Portfolio</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">. We establish a general allowance for loans that are not individually impaired by segregating the loans by loan category and assigning allowance percentages based on our historical loss experience adjusted for current environmental factors such as, delinquency trends and management&#8217;s evaluation of the collectability of the loan portfolio. The allowance may be adjusted for significant factors that, in management&#8217;s judgment, affect the collectability of the portfolio as of the evaluation date. These significant factors may include changes in lending policies and procedures, changes in existing general economic and business conditions affecting our primary market area, credit quality trends, collateral value, loan volumes and concentrations, seasoning of the loan portfolio, recent loss experience in particular segments of the portfolio, duration of the current business cycle and bank regulatory examination results. The applied loss factors are re-evaluated quarterly to help ensure their relevance in the current real estate environment. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">As an integral part of their examination process, the OCC will periodically review our allowance for loan losses, and may require that we recognize additions to the allowance based on their judgments of information available to them at the time of their examination. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Allowance for Loan Losses</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> The following table sets forth activity in our allowance for loan losses for the years indicated. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 12pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Allocation of Allowance for Loan Losses. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The following table sets forth the allowance for loan losses allocated by loan category and the percent of loans in each category to total allocated loans at the dates indicated. The allowance for loan losses allocated to each category is not necessarily indicative of future losses in any particular category and does not restrict the use of the allowance to absorb losses in other categories. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, our allowance for loan losses represented <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">1.43</font>% of gross loans and <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">48.76</font>% of non-performing loans. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Although we believe that we use the best information available to establish the allowance for loan losses, future adjustments to the allowance may be necessary and results of operations could be adversely or positively affected if circumstances differ substantially from the assumptions used in making our determinations. Furthermore, while we believe we have established our allowance for loan losses in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America, there can be no assurance that regulators, in reviewing our loan portfolio, will not request us to increase our allowance for loan losses. In addition, because future events affecting borrowers and collateral cannot be predicted with certainty, there can be no assurance that the existing allowance for loan losses is adequate or that increases will not be necessary should the quality of any loan deteriorate as a result of the factors discussed above. Any material increase in the allowance for loan losses may adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Investment Activities </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">General</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">. We utilize mortgage-backed and other securities in our asset/liability management. In making investment decisions, management considers, among other things, our yield and interest rate objectives, our interest rate risk and credit risk position, our loan volume, and our liquidity and cash flow. As of December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, all of our investment securities were available-for-sale and were issued by U.S. government sponsored entities which the government has affirmed its commitment to support. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We maintain minimum levels of liquid assets to help ensure we have adequate cash to fund anticipated needs. Liquidity may increase or decrease depending upon the availability of funds and comparative yields on investments in relation to the return on loans. Cash flow projections are reviewed and updated regularly to assure that adequate liquidity is maintained. Our level of liquidity is a result of management&#8217;s asset/liability strategy. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Government sponsored entities residential mortgage-backed securities and other government sponsored entity securities carry a yield generally lower than that of the corresponding type of residential loan. Accordingly, if the proportion of our assets consisting of government sponsored entities residential mortgage-backed securities and other government sponsored entity securities increases, our asset yields would likely be somewhat adversely affected. We will evaluate government sponsored entity securities purchases in the future based on our asset/liability objectives, market conditions and alternative investment opportunities. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Investment Securities Portfolio. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The following table sets forth the composition of our investment securities portfolio at the dates indicated, excluding stock of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago. All securities were held for sale at the dated indicated. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Other Securities. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">During recent years, our investment in securities other than residential mortgage-backed securities, cash and cash equivalents, and Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago stock have been quite limited. However, in the future, depending on asset/liability management considerations and market considerations, we may determine to invest in other securities including securities issued by the U.S. Treasury and U.S Government agencies, corporate debt securities and, to a lesser extent, corporate equity securities. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Sources of Funds </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">General. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Deposits have traditionally been our primary source of funds for use in lending and investment activities. From time to time we have also used borrowings, primarily Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago advances, to supplement cash flow needs, lengthen the maturities of liabilities for interest rate risk purposes and to manage the cost of funds. In addition, we receive funds from scheduled loan payments, investment maturities, loan prepayments, retained earnings and income on earning assets. While scheduled loan payments and income on earning assets are relatively stable sources of funds, deposit inflows and outflows can vary widely and are influenced by prevailing interest rates, market conditions and levels of competition. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Deposits.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> Historically, our deposits are generated primarily from residents within our primary market area. We offer a selection of deposit accounts, including demand accounts, NOW accounts, money market accounts, savings accounts and certificates of deposit. Deposit account terms vary, with the principal differences being the minimum balance required, the amount of time the funds must remain on deposit and the interest rate. We have not accepted brokered deposits in the past. Interest rates paid, maturity terms, service fees and withdrawal penalties are established on a periodic basis. Deposit rates and terms are based primarily on current operating strategies and market rates, liquidity requirements, rates paid by competitors and growth goals. Personalized customer service and long-standing relationships with customers are relied upon to attract and retain deposits. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The flow of deposits is influenced significantly by general economic conditions, changes in interest rates and competition. Our ability to gather deposits is impacted by the competitive market in which we operate which includes numerous financial institutions of varying sizes offering a wide range of products. We often use promotional rates to meet asset/liability and market segment goals. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The variety of deposit accounts offered allows us to be competitive in obtaining funds and responding to changes in consumer demand. Based on our experience, we believe that statement savings, demand and NOW accounts may be somewhat more stable sources of deposits than certificates of deposits. However, it can be difficult to attract and maintain such deposits at favorable interest rates under current market conditions. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">As we focus on providing business banking products and services and through meaningful and directed relationship development, we try to capture additional low cost deposits, such as commercial demand deposits and savings accounts, not for profit demand deposit accounts and commercial money market accounts. &nbsp;Further, we endeavor to develop a &#8220;house-holding&#8221; approach to relationship management. &nbsp;By this we mean developing whole banking relationships that include not only business related accounts, but also the related personal and employee based accounts. Additionally, we will require depository accounts with borrowing relationships. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class="pageBreak">
<div class=" ParaMarked">

<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Subsidiary Activities </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Ben Franklin Financial has no direct or indirect subsidiaries other than Ben Franklin Bank of Illinois. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Personnel </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we had a total of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">26</font> full-time employees. Our employees are not represented by any collective bargaining group. Management believes that we have good working relationships with our employees. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt; text-align: center;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">SUPERVISION AND REGULATION </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">General </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Ben Franklin Bank is examined and supervised by the OCC and is subject to examination by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. This regulation and supervision establishes a comprehensive framework of activities in which an institution may engage and is intended primarily for the protection of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation&#8217;s deposit insurance fund and depositors, and not for the protection of security holders. Under this system of federal regulation, financial institutions are periodically examined to ensure that they satisfy applicable standards with respect to matters such as their capital adequacy, assets, management, earnings, liquidity and sensitivity to market interest rates. Ben Franklin Bank also is regulated to a lesser extent by the Federal Reserve Board, governing reserves to be maintained against deposits and other matters. The OCC examines Ben Franklin Bank and prepares reports for the consideration of our board of directors on any operating deficiencies. Ben Franklin Bank&#8217;s relationship with its depositors and borrowers also is regulated to a great extent by federal law and, to a much lesser extent, state law, especially in matters concerning the ownership of deposit accounts and the form and content of Ben Franklin Bank&#8217;s loan documents. Ben Franklin Bank also is a member of and owns stock in the Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago, which is <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> of the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">twelve</font> regional banks in the Federal Home Loan Bank System. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">As a savings and loan holding company, the Company is required to comply with the rules and regulations of the Federal Reserve Board. It is required to file certain reports with the Federal Reserve Board and is subject to examination by and the enforcement authority of the Federal Reserve Board. The Company is also subject to the rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission under the federal securities laws. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Any change in applicable laws or regulations, whether by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the OCC, the Federal Reserve Board or Congress, could have a material adverse impact on the operations and financial performance of Ben Franklin Financial and Ben Franklin Bank. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Set forth below is a brief description of material regulatory requirements that are or will be applicable to the Company and Ben Franklin Bank. The description is limited to certain material aspects of the statutes and regulations addressed, and is not intended to be a complete description of such statutes and regulations and their effects on the Company and Ben Franklin Bank. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Consent Order and Board Resolutions </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">On November</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">25</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font> the Bank entered into a revised Consent Order (the &#8220;New Order&#8221;) with the OCC that reduces the Bank&#8217;s regulatory compliance burden. Concurrent with the execution of the New Order, the Bank&#8217;s prior Consent Order (the &#8220;Old Order&#8221;) entered into between the Bank and the OCC dated December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">19</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2012</font> was terminated. The New Order is comprised of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> substantive articles as opposed to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font> substantive articles under the Old Order. The New Order reduced the Bank&#8217;s minimum required Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> leverage capital ratio to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">8</font>% from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">9</font>% under the Old Consent Order and its minimum total risk-based capital ratio to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font>% from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">13</font>% under the Old Order. The New Order requires the Bank to revise its current capital plan to include a capital distribution policy. Additionally, the New Order requires the Bank to revise its strategic plan to identify parameters and triggers which would cause the board of directors to market the Bank for merger or sale, in the event it failed to meet the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">8</font>% and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font>% capital requirements under the New Order. The New Order continues to require quarterly reporting to the OCC and board monitoring requirements. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A federal savings bank is considered to be in &#8220;troubled condition&#8221; if (i)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it has a composite rating of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">4</font> or <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">5</font> under the Uniform Financial Institutions Rating System, (ii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it is informed in writing by the OCC that it has been designated as being in troubled condition, or (iii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it is subject to a formal enforcement order with the OCC, such as the New Order. Consequently, Ben Franklin Bank is in troubled condition, and is subject to additional regulatory restrictions that require it to: </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

This resolution remains in effect for the Company with the completion of the reorganization in January 2015. <p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Business Activities </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A federal savings bank derives its lending and investment powers from the Home Owners&#8217; Loan Act, as amended, and the regulations of the OCC. Under these laws and regulations, Ben Franklin Bank may originate mortgage loans secured by residential and commercial real estate, commercial business loans and consumer loans, and it may invest in certain types of debt securities and certain other assets. Certain types of lending, such as commercial and consumer loans, are subject to aggregate limits calculated as a specified percentage of Ben Franklin Bank&#8217;s capital or assets. Ben Franklin Bank also may establish service corporation subsidiaries that may engage in a variety of activities, including some that are not otherwise permissible for Ben Franklin Bank, including real estate investment and securities and insurance brokerage. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Dodd-Frank Act removed federal statutory restrictions on the payment of interest on commercial demand deposit accounts, effective July</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">21</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2011</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Loans-to-<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">One</font>-Borrower </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We generally may not make a loan or extend credit to a single or related group of borrowers in excess of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">15</font>% of our unimpaired capital and unimpaired surplus. An additional amount may be lent, equal to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font>% of unimpaired capital and unimpaired surplus, if the loan is secured by readily marketable collateral, which is defined to include certain financial instruments and bullion, but generally does not include real estate. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, based on the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">15</font>% limitation, our loans-to-<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>-borrower limit was approximately $1.3&nbsp;million. On the same date, we had four borrowers with outstanding balances and or commitments in excess of this amount. &nbsp;These outstanding balances or commitments were within the limits at the time they were originated.</font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Qualified Thrift Lender Test </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We are required to satisfy a qualified thrift lender (&#8220;QTL&#8221;) test, which required us to either qualify as a &#8220;domestic building and loan&#8221; association as defined by the Internal Revenue Code or maintain at least <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">65</font>% of our &#8220;portfolio assets&#8221; in &#8220;qualified thrift investments.&#8221; &#8220;Qualified thrift investments&#8221; consist primarily of residential mortgages and related investments, including mortgage-backed and related securities. &#8220;Portfolio assets&#8221; generally means total assets less specified liquid assets up to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font>% of total assets, goodwill and other intangible assets and the value of property used to conduct business. A savings institution that fails the qualified thrift lender test must operate under specified restrictions. The Dodd-Frank Act made noncompliance with the QTL test also subject to agency enforcement action for a violation of law. As of December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we maintained <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">96.6</font>% of our portfolio assets in qualified thrift investments and, therefore, we satisfied the QTL test. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Standards for Safety and Soundness </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Federal law requires each federal banking agency to prescribe for insured depository institutions under its jurisdiction standards relating to, among other things, internal controls, information systems and internal audit systems, loan documentation, credit underwriting, interest rate risk exposure, asset growth, employee compensation, and other operational and managerial standards as the agency deems appropriate. The federal banking agencies adopted Interagency Guidelines Prescribing Standards for Safety and Soundness to implement the safety and soundness standards required under federal law. The guidelines set forth the safety and soundness standards that the federal banking agencies use to identify and address problems at insured depository institutions before capital becomes impaired. If the appropriate federal banking agency determines that an institution fails to meet any standard prescribed by the guidelines, the agency may require the institution to submit to the agency an acceptable plan to achieve compliance with the standard. If an institution fails to submit or implement an acceptable plan, the appropriate federal banking agency may issue an enforceable order requiring correction of the deficiencies. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Capital Requirements </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Federal regulations require savings associations to meet several minimum capital standards: a common equity Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital to risk-based assets ratio of <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">4.5</font>%, a Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital to risk-based assets ratio of <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">6.0</font>%, a total capital to risk-based assets of <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.0</font>%, and a <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">4.0</font>% Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital to total assets leverage ratio. The existing capital requirements were effective January</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font> and are the result of regulations implementing recommendations of the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and certain requirements of the Dodd-Frank Act. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class="pageBreak">
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table style="width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td class="pgno" style="padding: 0px; text-align: center;"><font style="font-size: 10pt; font-family: 'times new roman', times;" class="pageno"><font class='pageno'>27</font></font></td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>

<div style="page-break-before: always; font-size: 10pt; text-align: left;"><a href="#TOC"><font style="font-family: 'times new roman', times; font-size: 10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a></div>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Risk-based capital standards for savings associations require the maintenance of common equity Tier</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital, Tier</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital and total capital to risk-weighted assets of at least <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">4.5</font>%, <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">6.0</font>% and <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.0</font>%, respectively. In determining the amount of risk-weighted assets, all assets, including certain off-balance sheet assets, are multiplied by a risk-weight factor assigned by the regulations based on the risks believed inherent in the type of asset. Common equity Tier</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital is generally defined as common stockholders&#8217; equity and retained earnings. Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital is generally defined as common equity Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> and additional Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital. Additional Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital includes certain noncumulative perpetual preferred stock and related surplus and minority interests in equity accounts of consolidated subsidiaries. Total capital includes Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital (common equity Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital plus additional Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital) and Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font> capital. Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font> capital is comprised of capital instruments and related surplus, meeting specified requirements, and may include cumulative preferred stock and long-term perpetual preferred stock, mandatory convertible securities, intermediate preferred stock and subordinated debt. Also included in Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font> capital is the allowance for loan and lease losses limited to a maximum of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.25</font>% of risk-weighted assets and, for institutions that have exercised an opt-out election regarding the treatment of Accumulated other comprehensive income, up to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">45</font>% of net unrealized gains on available-for-sale equity securities with readily determinable fair market values. Calculation of all types of regulatory capital is subject to deductions and adjustments specified in the regulations. In assessing an institution&#8217;s capital adequacy, the OCC takes into consideration, not only these numeric factors, but qualitative factors as well, and has the authority to establish higher capital requirements for individual associations where necessary. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In addition to establishing the minimum regulatory capital requirements, the regulations limit capital distributions and certain discretionary bonus payments to management if the institution does not hold a &#8220;capital conservation buffer&#8221; consisting of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2.5</font>% of common equity Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital to risk-weighted asset above the amount necessary to meet its minimum risk-based capital requirements. The capital conservation buffer requirement is being phased in beginning January</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> at <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">0.625</font>% of risk-weighted assets and increasing each year until fully implemented at <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2.5</font>% on January</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2019</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">On November</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">25</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>, Ben Franklin Bank entered into a New Order with the OCC (see &#8220;&#8212;Consent Order and Board Resolutions Above&#8221; above) which included a requirement to maintain a total risk-based capital ratio of at least 12% and a minimum Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> leverage capital ratio of at least 8%. As a result of entering into the New Order to achieve and maintain specific capital levels, Ben Franklin Bank&#8217;s capital classification under the Prompt Corrective Action rules was &#8220;adequately capitalized&#8221; at December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, Ben Franklin Bank had a Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> leverage capital level of $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">7.5</font> million, or <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">9.3</font>% which met the requirement of the minimum capital ratio established by the New Order. The Bank had a total risk-based capital level of $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.2</font> million, or <font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">14.5</font>% of risk-weighted assets which met the requirement of the New Order. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Prompt Corrective Regulatory Action </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Under prompt corrective action regulations, the Federal Reserve Board is authorized and, under certain circumstances, required to take supervisory actions against undercapitalized member banks. For this purpose, a member bank is placed in <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> of the following <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">five</font> categories based on the bank&#8217;s capital: </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
