<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Capital Distributions </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Federal regulations restrict capital distributions by savings institutions, which include cash dividends, stock repurchases and other transactions charged to the capital account of a savings institution. A federal savings institution must file an application with the OCC for approval of the capital distribution if: </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="border-collapse: collapse; margin-left: 0pt; width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: middle; width: 8%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 4%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &#8226; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 1%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> the total capital distributions for the applicable calendar year exceeds the sum of the institution&#8217;s net income for that year to date plus the institution&#8217;s retained net income for the preceding <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> years that is still available to be paid as a dividend; </font></p>
</td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="border-collapse: collapse; margin-left: 0pt; width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: middle; width: 8%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 4%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &#8226; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 1%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> the institution would not be at least adequately capitalized following the distribution; </font></p>
</td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="border-collapse: collapse; margin-left: 0pt; width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: middle; width: 8%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 4%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &#8226; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 1%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> the distribution would violate any applicable statute, regulation, agreement or written regulatory condition; or </font></p>
</td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="border-collapse: collapse; margin-left: 0pt; width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td style="vertical-align: middle; width: 8%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 4%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &#8226; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top; width: 1%;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> &nbsp; </font></p>
</td>
<td style="vertical-align: top;">
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> the institution is not eligible for expedited review of its filings (i.e., generally, institutions that do not have safety and soundness, compliance and Community Reinvestment Act ratings in the top <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> categories or fail a capital requirement). </font></p>
</td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A savings institution that is a subsidiary of a holding company, which is the case with Ben Franklin Bank, must file a notice with the Federal Reserve Board at least <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">30</font> days before the board of directors declares a dividend or approves a capital distribution, and must receive Federal Reserve Board non-objection to the payment of the dividend. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Applications or notices may be denied if the institution would be undercapitalized after the dividend, the proposed dividend raises safety and soundness concerns or the proposed dividend would violate a law, regulation enforcement order or regulatory condition. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In the event a savings institution&#8217;s capital falls below its regulatory requirements or is notified by the regulatory agency that it is in need of more than normal supervision, its ability to make capital distributions would be restricted. In addition, any proposed capital distribution could be prohibited if the regulatory agency determines that the distribution would constitute an unsafe or unsound practice. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Transactions with Related Parties </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A savings institution&#8217;s authority to engage in transactions with related parties or &#8220;affiliates&#8221; is limited by Sections <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">23</font>A and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">23</font>B of the Federal Reserve Act and the Federal Reserve Board&#8217;s Regulation W. The term &#8220;affiliate&#8221; generally means any company that controls or is under common control with an institution, including Ben Franklin Financial and its non-savings institution subsidiaries. Applicable law limits the aggregate amount of &#8220;covered&#8221; transactions with any individual affiliate, including loans to the affiliate, to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font>% of the capital and surplus of the savings institution. The aggregate amount of covered transactions with all affiliates is limited to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font>% of the savings institution&#8217;s capital and surplus. Certain covered transactions with affiliates, such as loans to or guarantees issued on behalf of affiliates, are required to be secured by specified amounts of collateral. Purchasing low quality assets from affiliates is generally prohibited. Regulation W also provides that transactions with affiliates, including covered transactions, must be on terms and under circumstances, including credit standards, that are substantially the same or at least as favorable to the institution as those prevailing at the time for comparable transactions with non-affiliated companies. In addition, savings institutions are prohibited by law from lending to any affiliate that is engaged in activities that are not permissible for bank holding companies and no savings institution may purchase the securities of any affiliate other than a subsidiary. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Our authority to extend credit to executive officers, directors or <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font>% or greater stockholders (&#8220;insiders&#8221;), as well as entities controlled by these persons, is governed by Sections</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">22</font>(g) and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">22</font>(h) of the Federal Reserve Act and Federal Reserve Board Regulation</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">O. Among other things, loans to insiders must be made on terms substantially the same as those offered to unaffiliated individuals and not involve more than the normal risk of repayment. There is an exception for bank-wide lending programs that do not discriminate in favor of insiders. Regulation</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">O also places individual and aggregate limits on the amount of loans that may be made to insiders based, in part, on the </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class="pageBreak">
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table style="width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td class="pgno" style="padding: 0px; text-align: center;"><font style="font-size: 10pt; font-family: 'times new roman', times;" class="pageno"><font class='pageno'>29</font></font></td>
</tr>

</table>
</div>
<hr style="border-bottom-color: #000000; border-top-color: #000000; color: #000000; background-color: #000000;"></hr>
<div style="page-break-before: always; font-size: 10pt; text-align: left;"><a href="#TOC"><font style="font-family: 'times new roman', times; font-size: 10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a></div>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">institution&#8217;s capital position, and requires that certain prior board approval procedures be followed. Extensions of credit to executive officers are subject to additional restrictions on the types and amounts of loans that may be made. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we were in compliance with these regulations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Enforcement </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The OCC has primary enforcement responsibility over federal savings institutions, including the authority to bring enforcement action against &#8220;institution-related parties,&#8221; which includes officers, directors, certain stockholders, and attorneys, appraisers and accountants who knowingly or recklessly participate in wrongful action likely to have an adverse effect on an institution. Formal enforcement action may range from the issuance of a capital directive or cease and desist order to removal of officers or directors of the institution, receivership, conservatorship or the termination of deposit insurance. Civil penalties cover a wide range of violations and actions, and range up to $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">25,000</font> per day, unless a finding of reckless disregard is made, in which case penalties may be as high as $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.0</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">million per day. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Deposit Insurance </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Ben Franklin Bank is a member of the Deposit Insurance Fund, which is administered by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Deposit accounts in Ben Franklin Bank are insured up to a maximum of $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">250,000</font> for each separately insured depositor. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation assesses deposit insurance premiums on all insured depository institutions. Under the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation&#8217;s risk-based assessment system, insured institutions are assigned to risk categories based on supervisory evaluations, regulatory capital levels and certain other factors. An institution&#8217;s assessment rate depends upon the category to which it is assigned and certain adjustments specified by Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation regulations, with institutions that are deemed less risky paying lower rates. Assessment rates (inclusive of possible adjustments) currently range from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6.67pt; vertical-align: super;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6.67pt; vertical-align: super;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">/</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6.67pt; vertical-align: sub;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">45</font> basis points of each institution&#8217;s total assets less tangible capital. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation may increase or decrease the range of assessments uniformly, except that no adjustment can deviate more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> basis points from the</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"> base assessment rate without notice and comment rulemaking. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation&#8217;s current system represents a change, required by the Dodd-Frank Act, from its prior practice of basing the assessment on an institution&#8217;s aggregate deposits. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In addition to the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation assessments, the Financing Corporation is authorized to impose and collect, through the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, assessments for anticipated payments, issuance costs and custodial fees on bonds issued by the Financing Corporation in the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1980</font>s to recapitalize the former Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation. The bonds issued by the Financing Corporation are <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> to mature in <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2017</font> through <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2019</font>. For the quarter ended December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, the annualized Financing Corporation assessment was equal to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">0.6</font> basis points of total assets less tangible capital. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Dodd-Frank Act increased the minimum target ratio for the Deposit Insurance Fund from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.15</font>% of estimated insured deposits to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.35</font>% of estimated insured deposits, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation must achieve the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.35</font>% ratio by September</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">30</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2020</font>. Insured institutions with assets of $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font> billion or more are required to fund the increase. The Dodd-Frank Act also eliminated the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.5</font>% maximum fund ratio, and instead gives the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation discretion to determine the maximum fund ratio. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation has exercised this discretion by establishing a long-term fund ratio of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2</font>%. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation has authority to increase insurance assessments. Any significant increases would have an adverse effect on the results of operations of Ben Franklin Bank. Management cannot predict what assessment rates will be in the future. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Insurance of deposits may be terminated by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation upon a finding that an institution has engaged in unsafe or unsound practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition to continue operations or has violated any applicable law, regulation, rule, order or condition imposed by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. Management of Ben Franklin Bank does not know of any practice, condition or violation that may lead to termination of our deposit insurance. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Federal Home Loan Bank System </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Ben Franklin Bank is a member of the Federal Home Loan Bank System, which consists of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">11</font> regional Federal Home Loan Banks. The Federal Home Loan Bank System provides a central credit facility primarily for member institutions. As a member of the Federal Home Loan Bank of Chicago, we are required to acquire and hold a specified amount of shares of capital stock in the Federal Home Loan Bank. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Community Reinvestment Act and Fair Lending Laws </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Savings institutions have a responsibility under the Community Reinvestment Act and related regulations to help meet the credit needs of their communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods. An institution&#8217;s failure to comply with the provisions of the Community Reinvestment Act could, at a minimum, result in regulatory restrictions on certain activities such as branching and acquisitions. Ben Franklin Bank received a &#8220;Satisfactory&#8221; Community Reinvestment Act rating in its most recent examination. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Other Regulations </font></p>

<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Holding Company Regulation </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Company is a unitary savings and loan holding company subject to regulation and supervision by the Federal Reserve Board. The Federal Reserve Board has enforcement authority over the Company and its non-savings institution subsidiaries. Among other things, this authority permits the Federal Reserve Board to restrict or prohibit activities that are determined to be a risk to Ben Franklin Bank. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">As a savings and loan holding company, the Company&#8217;s activities will be limited to those activities permissible by law for financial holding companies, under certain circumstances described below, bank holding companies under section <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">4</font>(c)(<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">8</font>) of the Bank Holding Company Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1956</font>, as amended, or multiple savings and loan holding companies. A financial holding company may engage in activities that are financial in nature, incidental to financial activities or complementary to a financial activity. Such activities include lending activities, insurance and underwriting equity securities. A savings and loan holding company must elect such status in order to engage in activities permissible for a financial holding company, must meet the qualitative requirements for a bank holding company to qualify as a financial holding company and conduct the activities in accordance with the requirements that would apply to a financial holding company&#8217;s conduct of the activity. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Federal law prohibits a savings and loan holding company, directly or indirectly, or through <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> or more subsidiaries, from acquiring more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">5</font>% of another savings institution or savings and loan holding company without prior written approval of the Federal Reserve Board, and from acquiring or retaining control of any depository institution not insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. In evaluating applications by holding companies to acquire savings institutions, the Federal Reserve Board must consider such things as the financial and managerial resources and future prospects of the company and institutions involved, the effect of the acquisition on and the risk to the federal deposit insurance fund, the convenience and needs of the community and competitive factors. A savings and loan holding company may not acquire a savings institution in another state and hold the target institution as a separate subsidiary unless it is a supervisory acquisition under Section</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">13</font>(k) of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act or the law of the state in which the target is located authorizes such acquisitions by out-of-state companies. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Savings and loan holding companies historically have not been subject to consolidated regulatory capital requirements. However, the Dodd-Frank Act requires the Federal Reserve Board to set for all depository institution holding companies minimum consolidated capital levels that are as stringent as those required for the insured depository subsidiaries. The components of Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital are restricted to capital instruments that are currently considered to be Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> capital for insured depository institutions, which excludes instruments such as trust preferred securities and cumulative preferred stock. Instruments issued before May</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">19</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2010</font> are grandfathered for companies with consolidated assets of $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">15</font> billion or less. The final capital rule discussed above implements the consolidated capital requirements for savings and loan holding companies effective January</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Dodd-Frank Act extended the &#8220;source of strength&#8221; doctrine to savings and loan holding companies. That doctrine requires holding companies to act as a source of strength to their subsidiary depository institutions by providing capital, liquidity and other support in times of financial stress. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Federal Reserve Board has issued a policy statement regarding the payment of dividends and the repurchase of shares of common stock by bank holding companies and savings and loan holding companies. In general, the policy provides that dividends should be paid only out of current earnings and only if the prospective rate of earnings retention by the holding company appears consistent with the organization&#8217;s capital needs, asset quality and overall financial condition. Regulatory guidance provides for prior regulatory review of capital distributions in certain circumstances such as where the company&#8217;s net income for the past <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font> quarters, net of dividends previously paid over that period, is insufficient to fully fund the dividend or the company&#8217;s overall rate of earnings retention is inconsistent with the company&#8217;s capital needs and overall financial condition. The ability of a holding company to pay dividends may be restricted if a subsidiary bank becomes undercapitalized. The guidance also states that a holding company should notify the Federal Reserve Board supervisory staff prior to redeeming or repurchasing common stock or perpetual preferred stock if the holding company is experiencing financial weaknesses or if the repurchase or redemption would result in a net reduction, as of the end of a quarter, in the amount of such equity instruments outstanding compared with the beginning of the quarter in which the redemption or repurchase occurred. These regulatory policies may affect the ability of Ben Franklin Financial to pay dividends, repurchase shares of common stock or otherwise engage in capital distributions. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Federal Securities Laws </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Company&#8217;s common stock is registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission and is subject to the information, proxy solicitation, insider trading restrictions and other requirements under the Securities Exchange Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1934</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The registration under the Securities Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1933</font> of shares of common stock issued in the Company&#8217;s public offering does not cover the resale of those shares. Shares of common stock purchased by persons who are not affiliates of Ben Franklin Financial may be resold without registration. Shares purchased by an affiliate of the Company will be subject to the resale restrictions of Rule <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">144</font> under the Securities Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1933</font>. If the Company meets the current public information requirements of Rule <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">144</font> under the Securities Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1933</font>, each affiliate of the Company that complies with the other conditions of Rule <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">144</font>, including those that require the affiliate&#8217;s sale to be aggregated with those of other persons, would be able to sell in the public market, without registration, a number of shares not to exceed, in any <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">three</font>-month period, the greater of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>% of the outstanding shares of the Company, or the average weekly volume of trading in the shares during the preceding <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font> calendar weeks. In the future, the Company may permit affiliates to have their shares registered for sale under the Securities Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1933</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Sarbanes-Oxley Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2002</font> </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2002</font> addresses, among other issues, corporate governance, auditing and accounting, executive compensation, and enhanced and timely disclosure of corporate information. We have existing policies, procedures and systems designed to comply with these regulations, and we review and document such policies, procedures and systems to ensure continued compliance with these regulations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Emerging Growth Company Status </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Jumpstart Our Business Startups Act (the &#8220;JOBS Act&#8221;), which was enacted in April 2012, has made numerous changes to the federal securities laws to facilitate access to capital markets. Under the JOBS Act, a company with total annual gross revenues of less than $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.0</font> billion during its most recently completed fiscal year qualifies as an &#8220;emerging growth company.&#8221; The Company qualifies as an emerging growth company under the JOBS Act. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">An &#8220;emerging growth company&#8221; may choose not to hold stockholder votes to approve annual executive compensation (more frequently referred to as &#8220;say-on-pay&#8221; votes) or executive compensation payable in connection with a merger (more frequently referred to as &#8220;say-on-golden parachute&#8221; votes). An emerging growth company also is not subject to the requirement that its auditors attest to the effectiveness of the company&#8217;s internal control over </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">financial reporting, and can provide scaled disclosure regarding executive compensation; however, the Company will also not be subject to the auditor attestation requirement or additional executive compensation disclosure so long as it remains a &#8220;smaller reporting company&#8221; under Securities and Exchange Commission regulations (generally less than $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">75</font> million of voting and non-voting equity held by non-affiliates). Finally, an emerging growth company may elect to comply with new or amended accounting pronouncements in the same manner as a private company, but must make such election when the company is first required to file a registration statement. Such an election is irrevocable during the period a company is an emerging growth company. The Company has elected to comply with new or amended accounting pronouncements in the same manner as a private company. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A company loses emerging growth company status on the earlier of: (i)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the last day of the fiscal year of the company during which it had total annual gross revenues of $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.0</font> billion or more; (ii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the last day of the fiscal year of the issuer following the fifth anniversary of the date of the first sale of common equity securities of the company pursuant to an effective registration statement under the Securities Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1933</font>; (iii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the date on which such company has, during the previous <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">three</font>-year period, issued more than $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1.0</font> billion in non-convertible debt; or (iv)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">the date on which such company is deemed to be a &#8220;large accelerated filer&#8221; under Securities and Exchange Commission regulations (generally, at least $<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">700</font> million of voting and non-voting equity held by non-affiliates). </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Change in Control Regulations </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Under the Change in Bank Control Act, no person may acquire control of a savings and loan holding company such as the Company unless the Federal Reserve Board has been given <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">60</font> days&#8217; prior written notice and has not issued a notice disapproving the proposed acquisition, taking into consideration certain factors, including the financial and managerial resources of the acquirer and the competitive effects of the acquisition. Control, as defined under federal law, means ownership, control of or holding irrevocable proxies representing more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">25</font>% of any class of voting stock, control in any manner of the election of a majority of the institution&#8217;s directors, or a determination by the regulator that the acquirer has the power, directly or indirectly, to exercise a controlling influence over the management or policies of the institution. Acquisition of more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">10</font>% of any class of a savings and loan holding company&#8217;s voting stock constitutes a rebuttable determination of control under the regulations under certain circumstances including where, as will be the case with the Company, the issuer has registered securities under Section</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font> of the Securities Exchange Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1934</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In addition, federal regulations provide that no company may acquire control of a savings and loan holding company without the prior approval of the Federal Reserve Board. Any company that acquires such control becomes a &#8220;savings and loan holding company&#8221; subject to registration, examination and regulation by the Federal Reserve Board. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Federal Taxation </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">General</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Company and Ben Franklin Bank are subject to federal income taxation in the same general manner as other corporations, with some exceptions discussed below. &nbsp;During the past five years, one tax return is in the process of being audited. &nbsp;The following discussion of federal taxation is intended only to summarize certain pertinent federal income tax matters and is not a comprehensive description of the tax rules applicable to the Company or Ben Franklin Bank</font>.</p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Method of Accounting</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">For federal income tax purposes, we report income and expenses on the accrual method of accounting and use a tax year ending December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font> for filing federal and state income tax returns. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Bad Debt Reserves</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Prior to the Small Business Protection Act of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1996</font> (the &#8220;<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1996</font> Act&#8221;), Ben Franklin Bank was permitted to establish a reserve for bad debts and to make annual additions to the reserve. These additions could, within specified formula limits, be deducted in arriving at our taxable income. Ben Franklin Bank was required to use the specific charge off method in computing its bad debt deduction beginning with its <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1997</font> federal tax return. Savings institutions were required to recapture any excess reserves established after December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1987</font>. The reserve balance as of December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1987</font> is referred to as the base year reserve. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Taxable Distributions and Recapture</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Prior to the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1996</font> Act, federal tax bad debt reserves created prior to January</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1988</font> were subject to recapture into taxable income if the thrift institution failed to meet certain thrift asset and definitional tests. Federal legislation has eliminated these thrift-related recapture rules. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, our total federal and Illinois pre-<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1988</font> base year tax bad debt reserve was approximately $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">355,000</font>. Under current law, pre-<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1988</font> federal base year reserves remain subject to recapture if a thrift institution makes certain non-dividend distributions, repurchases any of its stock, pays dividends in excess of tax earnings and profits, or ceases to maintain a thrift or bank charter. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Alternative Minimum Tax</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Internal Revenue Code of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1986</font>, as amended, imposes an alternative minimum tax (&#8220;AMT&#8221;) at a rate of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font>% on a base of regular taxable income plus certain tax preferences (&#8220;alternative minimum taxable income&#8221; or &#8220;AMTI&#8221;). The AMT is payable to the extent such AMTI is in excess of an exemption amount and the AMT exceeds the regular income tax. Net operating losses can offset no more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">90</font>% of AMTI. Certain payments of AMT may be used as credits against regular tax liabilities in future years. We have not been subject to the AMT and have no such amounts available as credits for carryover. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Net Operating Loss Carryovers</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Generally we may carry back federal net operating losses to the preceding <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">two</font> taxable years and forward to the succeeding <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font> taxable years. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we have federal net operating losses of approximately $7.4&nbsp;million which are being carried forward and available to reduce future taxable income. These carryforwards expire beginning <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2030</font> through <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2036</font>. For financial reporting purposes, at December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we continue to maintain a valuation allowance established at December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2009</font>, based on our assessment of our ability to realize our net deferred tax asset <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> to continuing losses incurred. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Corporate Dividends-Received Deduction</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Company may exclude from its income <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">100</font>% of dividends received from Ben Franklin Bank as a member of the same affiliated group of corporations. The corporate dividends-received deduction is <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">80</font>% in the case of dividends received from corporations with which a corporate recipient does not file a consolidated return, and owns more than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font>% of the stock. A corporation receiving a dividend may deduct only <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">70</font>% of dividends if the corporation owns less than <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">20</font>% of the dividend paying corporation. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 18pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">State and Local Taxation </font></p>
<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic; font-weight: bold;">Illinois State Taxation</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-style: italic;">. </font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The Company and Ben Franklin Bank are required to file Illinois income tax returns and pay tax at a stated tax rate of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">9.5</font>% of Illinois taxable income. For these purposes, Illinois taxable income generally means federal taxable income subject to certain modifications, primarily the exclusion of interest income on United States obligations. As of December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we have Illinois net operating losses of approximately $9.2&nbsp;million which are being carried forward and available to reduce future taxable income. These carryforwards expire beginning <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2019</font> through <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2028</font>. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">As a Maryland business corporation, The Company is required to file an annual report with and pay franchise taxes to the state of Maryland. </font></p>

<p style="margin: 6pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Ben Franklin Bank is subject to a Consent Order with the OCC, including an individual minimum capital requirement that may adversely affect our operations and our financial performance. The Company has also adopted a board resolution requested by the Federal Reserve Board which, among other things, prohibit us from paying dividends, increasing our debt or redeeming shares of the Company&#8217;s stock without prior written approval from the Federal Reserve Board. Continued compliance with the Consent Order and board resolutions may restrict our operations and adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">On November</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">25</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2015</font> the Bank entered into a revised Consent Order (the &#8220;New Order&#8221;) with the OCC that reduces the Bank&#8217;s regulatory compliance burden. Concurrent with the execution of the New Order, the Bank&#8217;s prior Consent Order (the &#8220;Old Order&#8221;) entered into between the Bank and the OCC dated December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">19</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2012</font> was terminated. <p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Old Order. The New Order reduced the Bank&#8217;s minimum required Tier <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">1</font> leverage capital ratio to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">8</font>% from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">9</font>% under the Old Order and its minimum total risk-based capital ratio to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font>% from <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">13</font>% under the Old Order. The New Order requires the Bank to revise its current capital plan to include a capital distribution policy. Additionally, the New Order requires the Bank to revise its strategic plan to identify parameters and triggers which would cause the board of directors to market the Bank for merger or sale, in the event it failed to meet the <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">8</font>% and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">12</font>% capital requirements under the New Order. The New Order continues to require quarterly reporting to the OCC and board monitoring requirements. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A federal savings bank is considered to be in &#8220;troubled condition&#8221; if (i)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it has a composite rating of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">4</font> or <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">5</font> under the Uniform Financial Institutions Rating System, (ii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it is informed in writing by the OCC that it has been designated as being in troubled condition, or (iii)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">it is subject to a formal enforcement order with the OCC, such as the New Order. Consequently, Ben Franklin Bank is in troubled condition, and is subject to additional regulatory restrictions that require it to: </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The New Order requires that we make quarterly progress reports to the OCC as to our compliance with the requirements of the Consent Order. The requirements of the New Order will remain in effect until the OCC suspends or terminates the New Order. Failure to comply with the New Order could result in additional enforcement actions by the OCC. We have incurred significant expense in complying with the Old Order, and continued compliance with the New Order may restrict our operations or result in continued expense, either of which may adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. For more information regarding the New Order, see &#8220;Regulation and Supervision&#8212;Consent Order and Board Resolutions.&#8221; </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">On March</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">27</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2014</font>, Ben Franklin-Federal and Ben Franklin Financial, MHC adopted board resolutions requested by the Federal Reserve Board that prohibit us from paying dividends, increasing our debt or redeeming shares of Ben Franklin-Federal stock without prior written approval from the Federal Reserve Board. Continued compliance with the board resolutions may restrict our operations and adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations. Failure to comply with the board resolutions could result in additional enforcement actions by the Federal Reserve Board. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">We cannot determine when Ben Franklin Financial would no longer be subject to the New Order or conditions of the board resolutions. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Our business strategy, which contemplates asset and liability growth, including significant loan growth, was recently adopted and implemented and has not yet had the time to be proven successful. If we fail to grow or fail to manage our growth effectively, our financial condition and results of operations could be negatively affected. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">In January 2016, the Board of Directors of Ben Franklin Bank approved a strategic plan which was submitted it to the OCC for their supervisory non-objection in accordance with the New Order. The plan contemplates growth in assets and liabilities, including significant loan growth, over the next several years. Under the plan, we intend to increase our <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>-to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>- family, commercial and multi-family real estate loans, home equity lines of credit and, to a lesser extent, commercial business loans, while attracting favorably priced deposits. The plan includes the purchase of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family and multi-family loans to supplement our internal production to </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<div class="pageBreak">
<div class=" ParaMarked">
<table style="width: 100%;" width="100%">

<tr>
<td class="pgno" style="padding: 0px; text-align: center;"><font style="font-size: 10pt; font-family: 'times new roman', times;" class="pageno"><font class='pageno'>36</font></font></td>

<div style="page-break-before: always; font-size: 10pt; text-align: left;"><a href="#TOC"><font style="font-family: 'times new roman', times; font-size: 10pt;">Table of Contents</font></a></div>
</div>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">increase our interest income. The plan also includes a decrease in compensation and benefits primarily <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">due</font> to salary adjustments and staffing changes. Over the past several years we have incurred substantial additional expenses including salaries related to new lending officers and related support staff. Unless we can successfully implement our strategic plan, our financial condition and results of operations will continue to be negatively affected by these increased costs. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">The successful implementation of our strategic plan will require, among other things, that we increase our market share by attracting new customers that currently bank at other financial institutions in our market area. In addition, our ability to successfully grow will depend on several factors, including continued favorable market conditions, the competitive responses from other financial institutions in our market area, and our ability to maintain high asset quality as we increase our commercial and multi-family real estate loans, home equity lines of credit and commercial business loans. Growth opportunities may not be available and we may not be successful in implementing our business strategy. Further, it will take time to implement our business strategy, especially for our lenders to originate enough loans and for our branches to attract enough favorably priced deposits to generate the revenue needed to offset the associated expenses. In addition, the successful implementation of our business strategy may require that we raise additional capital, which may not be available on terms that allow us to successfully implement our plan. &nbsp; Assuming the successful execution of our business plan, we do not expect that we will return to profitability until fiscal <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2019</font>. We may be unsuccessful, however, in executing on our business plan and may not be able to return to profitability in the timeframe we expect, or at all.</font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">The implementation of our business strategy, which includes significant growth of our loan portfolio, may require that we raise additional capital. Such capital may not be available on terms that are consistent with our business strategy, which could cause our business strategy to fail. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp; &nbsp;We may need to raise additional capital in the future to support operations and the significant growth of our loan portfolio that is contemplated by our business strategy. Our ability to raise capital, if needed, will depend on conditions in the capital markets at that time, which are outside of our control and our financial performance. If we cannot raise additional capital when needed on terms that are consistent with the successful implementation of our business strategy, it would affect our operations and could cause our business strategy to be unsuccessful.</font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">If our problem assets increase, our results of operations may decline. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, our non-performing assets, which were also our classified assets, totaled $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">1.9</font> million or&nbsp;<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">2.7</font>% of our total assets and consisted of $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">345,000</font> of non-accrual troubled debt restructurings, $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">1.5</font> million of non-accrual loans, and $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">408,000</font> of repossessed assets.</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;Our problem assets adversely affect our net income in various ways. We do not record interest income on non-accrual loans or repossessed assets. Based on our estimate of the level of allowance for loan losses required, we record a provision for loan losses as a charge to earnings to maintain the allowance for loan losses at an appropriate level. We also write down the value of properties in our repossessed assets to reflect changing market values. Additionally, there are legal fees associated with the resolution of problem assets as well as carrying costs such as taxes, insurance and maintenance related to our repossessed assets. Further, the resolution of problem assets requires the active involvement of management, which could detract from the overall supervision of our operations and implementation of our business strategy. Finally, if our estimate of the allowance for loan losses is inadequate, we will have to increase the allowance accordingly. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Changes in interest rates could adversely affect our results of operations and financial condition. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Our results of operations and financial condition are significantly affected by changes in interest rates. Our results of operations depend substantially on our net interest income, which is the difference between the interest income we earn on our interest-earning assets, such as loans and securities, and the interest expense we pay on our interest-bearing liabilities, such as deposits and borrowings. Because our interest-bearing liabilities generally reprice or mature more quickly than our interest-earning assets, a sustained increase in interest rates generally would tend to reduce our interest income. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, a portion (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">16.9</font>%)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">of our loan portfolio was comprised of fixed-rate loans with remaining terms of over <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">15</font> years while a significant portion (<font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">62.9</font>%)</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">of our certificates of deposit had terms of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font> year or less. In the event that interest rates suddenly rise our interest expense may rise more quickly than our interest income. Consequently, we may experience a related decrease in our net interest income. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Changes in interest rates also may affect the average life of loans and mortgage-related securities. Decreases in interest rates can result in increased prepayments of loans and mortgage-related securities, as borrowers refinance to reduce their borrowing costs. Under these circumstances, we are subject to reinvestment risk to the extent that we are unable to reinvest the cash received from such prepayments at rates that are comparable to the rates on existing loans and securities. Additionally, increases in interest rates may decrease loan demand and make it more difficult for borrowers to repay adjustable-rate loans. Also, increases in interest rates may extend the life of fixed-rate assets, which would restrict our ability to reinvest in higher yielding alternatives, and may result in customers withdrawing certificates of deposit early so long as the early withdrawal penalty is less than the interest they could receive on a new investment. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<div class=" ParaMarked">

<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Changes in interest rates also affect the current fair value of our interest-earning securities portfolio. Generally, the value of our securities classified as available for sale changes inversely with changes in interest rates. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, the fair value of our portfolio of investment securities classified as available for sale totaled $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.2</font> million. At that date, net unrealized loss on these securities totaled $145. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Our business plan contemplates an increase in our origination of commercial and multi-family real estate loans and, to a lesser extent, commercial business loans, which carry greater credit risk than loans secured by owner occupied <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family real estate. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Pursuant to our strategic plan, we intend to increase our level of <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family, multi-family and commercial real estate loans and, to a lesser extent, our commercial business loan originations. Given their larger balances and the complexity of the underlying collateral, commercial and multi-family real estate loans generally expose a lender to greater credit risk than loans secured by owner occupied <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">one</font>- to <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">four</font>-family real estate. This increased credit risk is a result of several factors, including the concentration of principal in a limited number of loans and borrowers, the impact of local and general economic conditions on the borrower&#8217;s ability to repay the loan, and the increased difficulty of evaluating and monitoring these types of loans. Furthermore, the repayment of loans secured by commercial and multi-family properties typically depends upon the successful operation of the real property securing the loan. If the cash flow from the property is reduced, the borrower&#8217;s ability to repay the loan may be impaired. Commercial business loans expose us to additional risks since they typically are made on the basis of the borrower&#8217;s ability to make repayments from the cash flow of the borrower&#8217;s business and are secured by non-real estate collateral that may depreciate over time, may be illiquid and may fluctuate in value based on the success of the business. A secondary market for most types of commercial real estate, commercial business and multi-family loans is not readily liquid, so we have less opportunity to mitigate credit risk by selling part or all of our interest in these loans. If these loans become non-performing, we may have to increase our provision for loan losses which would negatively affect our results of operations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">Our small size makes it more difficult for us to compete. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Our small asset size makes it more difficult to compete with other community banks which are generally larger and can more easily afford to invest in the marketing and technologies needed to attract and retain customers. At December</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;"><font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">31</font>, <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2016</font>, we had $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">85.3</font></font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">&nbsp;</font><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">million of total assets, $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">62.3</font> million of loans receivable, net of the allowance for loan losses, $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.2</font> million of available-for-sale investment securities, $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">74.0</font> million of total deposits and $<font class="FactMarked Linked mceNonEditable">8.1</font> million of total equity. Because our principal source of income is the net interest income we earn on our loans and investments after deducting interest paid on deposits and other sources of funds, our ability to generate the revenues needed to cover our expenses and finance such investments is limited by the size of our loan and investment portfolios. Our small size also means that we are not always able to offer competitive salaries and benefits. In addition, our smaller customer base makes it relatively more difficult to generate significant noninterest income from other activities. Finally, as a smaller institution, we are disproportionately affected by the continually increasing costs of compliance with new banking and other regulations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt; font-weight: bold;">A worsening of economic conditions could result in increases in our level of non-performing loans and/or reduce demand for our products and services, which could have an adverse effect on our results of operations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 12pt 0pt 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">Although the U.S. economy has emerged from the severe recession that occurred in <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2008</font> and <font class="FactMarked mceNonEditable">2009</font>, economic growth has been slow and, until recently, unemployment levels remained high despite the Federal Reserve Board&#8217;s unprecedented efforts to encourage economic growth by maintaining low interest rates through its targeted federal funds rate and the purchase of U.S. Treasury and mortgage-backed securities. Recovery by many businesses has been impaired by lower consumer spending. If the Federal Reserve Board continues to increase the federal funds rate or more rapidly curtails its bond purchasing program, higher interest rates would likely result, which may reduce our loan originations, and housing markets and U.S. economic activity would be negatively affected. Our operations are significantly affected by national and local economic conditions. Substantially all of our loans are to businesses and individuals in the metropolitan Chicago area. Both of our branches and most of our deposit customers also are located in this area. A decline in the economies in which we operate could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations. </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 8pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>

<p style="margin: 0pt; text-indent: 8%;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 10pt;">A deterioration in economic conditions in the market areas we serve could result in the following consequences, any of which could have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition and results of operations: </font></p>
<p style="margin: 0pt;"><font style="font-family: 'Times New Roman'; font-size: 6pt;">&nbsp;</font></p>
